fetched_contents.text: Sample size, power and effect size revisited: simplified and practical approaches in pre-clinical, clinical and laboratory studies Abstract Calculating the sample size in scientific studies is one of the critical issues as regards the scientific contribution of the study. The sample size critically affects the hypothesis and the study design, and there is no straightforward way of calculating the effective sample size for reaching an accurate conclusion. Use of a statistically incorrect sample size may lead to inadequate results in both clinical and laboratory studies as well as resulting in time loss, cost, and ethical problems. This review holds two main aims. The first aim is to explain the importance of sample size and its relationship to effect size (ES) and statistical significance. The second aim is to assist researchers planning to perform sample size estimations by suggesting and elucidating available alternative software, guidelines and references that will serve different scientific purposes. Keywords: biostatistics, effect size, power analysis, sample size Introduction Statistical analysis is a crucial part of a research. A scientific study must include statistical tools in the study, beginning from the planning stage. Developed in the last 20-30 years, information technology, along with evidence-based medicine, increased the spread and applicability of statistical science. Although scientists have understood the importance of statistical analysis for researchers, a significant number of researchers admit that they lack adequate knowledge about statistical concepts and principles (1). In a study by West and Ficalora, more than two-thirds of the clinicians emphasized that “the level of biostatistics education that is provided to the medical students is not sufficient” (2). As a result, it was suggested that statistical concepts were either poorly understood or not understood at all (3, 4). Additionally, intentionally or not, researchers tend to draw conclusions that cannot be supported by the actual study data, often due to the misuse of statistics tools (5). As a result, a large number of statistical errors occur affecting the research results. Although there are a variety of potential statistical errors that might occur in any kind of scientific research, it has been observed that the sources of error have changed due to the use of dedicated software that facilitates statistics in recent years. A summary of main statistical errors frequently encountered in scientific studies is provided below (6-13): * Flawed and inadequate hypothesis; * Improper study design; * Lack of adequate control condition/group; * Spectrum bias; * Overstatement of the analysis results; * Spurious correlations; * Inadequate sample size; * Circular analysis (creating bias by selecting the properties of the data retrospectively); * Utilization of inappropriate statistical studies and fallacious bending of the analyses; * p-hacking (i.e. addition of new covariates post hoc to make P values significant); * Excessive interpretation of limited or insignificant results (subjectivism); * Confusion (intentionally or not) of correlations, relationships, and causations; * Faulty multiple regression models; * Confusion between P value and clinical significance; and * Inappropriate presentation of the results and effects (erroneous tables, graphics, and figures). Relationship among sample size, power, P value and effect size In this review, we will concentrate on the problems associated with the relationships among sample size, power, P value, and effect size (ES). Practical suggestions will be provided whenever possible. In order to understand and interpret the sample size, power analysis, effect size, and P value, it is necessary to know how the hypothesis of the study was formed. It is best to evaluate a study for Type I and Type II errors (Figure 1) through consideration of the study results in the context of its hypotheses (14-16). A statistical hypothesis is the researcher’s best guess as to what the result of the experiment will show. It states, in a testable form the proposition the researcher plans to examine in a sample to be able to find out if the proposition is correct in the relevant population. There are two commonly used types of hypotheses in statistics. These are the null hypothesis (H0) and the alternative (H1) hypothesis. Essentially, the H1 is the researcher’s prediction of what will be the situation of the experimental group after the experimental treatment is applied. The H0 expresses the notion that there will be no effect from the experimental treatment. Prior to the study, in addition to stating the hypothesis, the researcher must also select the alpha (α) level at which the hypothesis will be declared “supported”. The α represents how much risk the researcher is willing to take that the study will conclude H1 is correct when (in the full population) it is not correct (and thus, the null hypothesis is really true). In other words, alpha represents the probability of rejecting H0 when it actually is true. (Thus, the researcher has made an error by reporting that the experimental treatment makes a difference, when in fact, in the full population, that treatment has no effect.) The most common α level chosen is 0.05, meaning the researcher is willing to take a 5% chance that a result supporting the hypothesis will be untrue in the full population. However, other alpha levels may also be appropriate in some circumstances. For pilot studies, α is often set at 0.10 or 0.20. In studies where it is especially important to avoid concluding a treatment is effective when it actually is not, the alpha may be set at a much lower value; it might be set at 0.001 or even lower. Drug studies are examples for studies that often set the alpha at 0.001 or lower because the consequences of releasing an ineffective drug can be extremely dangerous for patients. fetched_contents.text: Suicide risk among individuals at Ultra-High Risk (UHR) of psychosis in a developing North African country: A 12-month naturalistic prospective cohort study from the TRIP project Highlights * • There is sufficient evidence that levels of suicidality are typically higher in individuals at ultra-high risk (UHR) for psychosis than in other clinical groups, such as help-seekers that reach UHR clinics but do not meet UHR criteria, and young people with first episode psychosis (FEP). * • The limited studies that have focused on suicidal thoughts and behaviors in UHR populations were predominantly cross-sectional and most of them have emerged from western countries. In addition, there is a lack of research on the role of potential and well-established causal factors for suicidality in this population. * • The present study contributes to the existing literature by providing novel prospective data on suicidality in UHR individuals from a previously unexplored country and region. * • Our findings support previous evidence that the prevalence of suicidal ideation and behavior in UHR individuals is concerning, and suggest that a routine monitoring of suicide risk by early intervention services is highly required. * • Some factors related to suicidal ideation and attempts have preliminarily been identified in the present study, and deserve further investigations, i.e. the duration of untreated illness, self-esteem levels, and the severity of psychotic symptoms. Abstract Background The limited studies that focused on suicidality in individuals at Ultra-High Risk (UHR) of psychosis were predominantly cross-sectional, emerging from Western countries. We aimed to examine suicide risk among Tunisian UHR and First Episode Psychosis (FEP) patients at baseline, and to evaluate the evolution and correlates of suicidal ideation over a 12-month period in the UHR group exclusively. Methods 35 UHR (aged 22.8 ± 4.0 years, 45.7% male) and 33 FEP (aged 27.3 ± 4.8 years, 63.6% male) participants were included. The Comprehensive Assessment of at Risk Mental States, the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS), The Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale, and The Multidimensional Scale of Perceived Social Support were used. Results No significant differences were found between the UHR and the FEP groups with regard to levels of suicidal ideation at baseline. Suicidal ideation scores showed a significant decrease over time in UHR participants (p=.014; η2=0.242). An increase in total PANSS scores at 1 year (Beta=0.03; p=.048; 95%CI 0.001, 0.060; η2=0.182) significantly increased suicidal ideation scores at 1 year in the UHR group. Conclusion Our findings contribute to the limited body of evidence on this topic by providing new prospective data from a population, country and region that has never been researched previously. Keywords Suicide risk ; Ultra-high risk ; Psychosis ; Tunisia ; Middle East and North Africa Introduction Suicide is amongst the leading causes of mortality in individuals diagnosed with schizophrenia (Olfson et al., 2015). They have a 4.5-fold increased risk of death by suicide as compared with the general population, with suicide risk being the highest in younger adult patients and decreasing gradually with age (Olfson et al., 2021). More specifically, risk of suicide and suicidal ideation in this population is particularly high around the onset of the disease (Pelizza et al., 2019). For example, it has been demonstrated that the annual rate of suicide during the first 5 years after first hospitalization is three times greater than after 10 to 16 years (Heilä et al., 2005; Nielssen and Large, 2009). Increased rates of suicidal thoughts and behavior have also been documented along the psychosis continuum; in adolescents with schizotypal traits (O′ Hare et al., 2021), in individuals with schizotypal personality disorder (Lentz et al., 2010), in non-clinical community individuals with psychotic experiences (Bromet et al., 2017), and in individuals at ultra-high risk (UHR) for psychosis (Bang et al., 2019; Fekih-Romdhane et al., 2021). Indeed, studies found that UHR subjects are at a heightened risk of suicide compared to the general population (Bang et al., 2019). A meta-analysis by Taylor et al. encompassing twenty-one UHR studies found an elevated prevalence of recent (2-week) suicidal ideation (66%), lifetime suicidal ideation (66%), and lifetime suicide attempts (18%) (Taylor et al., 2015). fetched_contents.text: Behavior of prediction performance metrics with rare events . Author manuscript; available in PMC: 2025 Dec 2. Abstract Objective Area under the receiving operator characteristic curve (AUC) is commonly reported alongside prediction models for binary outcomes. Recent articles have raised concerns that AUC might be a misleading measure of prediction performance in the rare event setting. This setting is common since many events of clinical importance are rare. We aimed to determine whether the bias and variance of AUC are driven by the number of events or the event rate. We also investigated the behavior of other commonly used measures of prediction performance, including positive predictive value, accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Study Design and Setting We conducted a simulation study to determine when or whether AUC is unstable in the rare event setting by varying the size of datasets used to train and evaluate prediction models. This plasmode simulation study was based on data from the Mental Health Research Network; the data contained 149 predictors and the outcome of interest, suicide attempt, which had event rate 0.92% in the original dataset. Results Our results indicate that poor AUC behavior—as measured by empirical bias, variability of cross-validated AUC estimates, and empirical coverage of confidence intervals—is driven by the number of events in a rare-event setting, not event rate. Performance of sensitivity is driven by the number of events, while that of specificity is driven by the number of non-events. Other measures, including positive predictive value and accuracy, depend on the event rate even in large samples. Conclusion AUC is reliable in the rare event setting provided that the total number of events is moderately large; in our simulations, we observed near zero bias with 1000 events. Keywords: Prediction, classification, machine learning, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, model evaluation, rare outcome Plain Language Summary Predicting self-harm or suicidal behavior is medically important for guiding clinicians in providing care to patients. Several research teams have developed and evaluated suicide risk prediction models based on health records data. Part of evaluating these models is calculating area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and other prediction performance metrics. Self-harm and suicide are rare events. Recent research has raised concerns with using AUC in rare-event settings. We aimed to determine whether having a sufficiently large dataset could remove these concerns. In our experiments, we found that AUC can be used without concern in settings with 1000 events or more. Thus, AUC is a valid measure of suicide risk prediction model performance in many large healthcare databases. 1. Introduction Clinical decision-making can be guided by prediction models that identify people at risk for negative health outcomes [1, 2, 3, 4]. Assessing model performance across many metrics is important. Selecting any one particular metric depends on how the model will be used in care [5, 6, 7]. Sensitivity and specificity [8], Brier score [9], and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC; 10] are all useful performance metrics when considering binary outcomes. Estimating and reporting prediction model performance in the rare event setting presents several challenges. First, even with a large number of observations, the absolute number of events may be small. In training predictive models, the number of events, not just the total sample size, is of importance [11]. Second, a small event rate impacts the behavior of some performance measures [12, 13]. AUC is often reported in the scientific literature to describe the performance of risk prediction models, as we and others have done when estimating models to predict suicide attempt [14, 15, 4, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23]. In our prior work, the per-visit 90-day suicide attempt rate was 0.62% for visits to mental health specialty clinics and 0.26% for general medical visits with mental health diagnoses; suicide deaths were even more rare, approximately 0.02% and 0.01%, respectively [4]. Recently, several studies have argued that AUC is a misleading and inappropriate measure of prediction model performance in the rare event setting [13, 12, 24, 25, 26]. In practice, when using large sample sizes, even with very rare events, AUC estimates of suicide risk prediction model performance have aligned with other performance metrics; in other words, multiple metrics yield similar conclusions about model adequacy and strength of risk discrimination [14, 18, 23]. This is contrary to concerns raised in recent literature [12, 25]. It is essential for researchers and decision makers to have a clear understanding of the statistical properties of performance measures in rare-outcome settings, including bias (including the potential for optimism) and stability (i.e., estimator variability), as many prediction models are developed to predict rare outcomes. In this paper we examine bias and variance of AUC and other performance metrics in a variety of settings, varying both the sample size and the event rate. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. We further assume a prediction model, f, trained on a sample from P, such that f returns a predicted probability of Y given X. Suicide prevalence is especially hard to estimate in UHR groups because the outcome is rare, yet the population is not representative of the general population, and study design constraints make long-term tracking difficult. The evidence suggests that suicide remains a major risk factor in UHR individuals, especially those at risk for psychosis, and that suicidality is typically higher in UHR groups than in other clinical cohorts such as first-episode psychosis or help-seekers who do not meet UHR criteria [N3-F3]. At the same time, suicide is rare enough that even among people at elevated risk, the absolute number of completed suicide events is small. The cited meta-analysis notes that UHR studies found elevated prevalence of recent suicidal ideation and lifetime suicidal ideation, but also notes that suicide-related studies are rare and often cross-sectional, with limited prospective data from non-Western settings [N3-F3]. This is consistent with the broader suicide literature, which shows that suicide rates can vary over time and can be influenced by many factors, but that the overall burden remains low enough that small changes in a study population can be difficult to distinguish from chance or measurement error [N2-R1][N2-R3][N2-R4].

A key reason prevalence is hard to estimate is ascertainment bias and underreporting. The suicide literature shows that suicide is a rare event, and when it is rare, studies must rely on careful ascertainment to capture events accurately. The cited prospective cohort study on UHR individuals emphasizes that there is limited research on suicidality in this population, and that most prior work has been cross-sectional and Western-focused [N3-F3]. That limitation matters because ascertainment can be incomplete in any cohort, and suicide events are particularly difficult to capture reliably when they are rare. The broader suicide measurement evidence also points to the importance of cohort studies and autopsied cohorts in estimating suicide rates [N2-R2], suggesting that without robust case ascertainment, observed prevalence may miss true events or overestimate them if linkage is weak. In UHR cohorts, the question of what counts as a suicide event matters because suicide is not always detected through routine clinical records alone; it may require linkage to death registries, coroner reports, or electronic health records [N6-R3][N6-R4]. Therefore, observed prevalence can be misleading if case ascertainment is imperfect or if suicide is underascertained in the source data [N2-R2][N6-R3].

Follow-up duration and attrition also make long-term prevalence estimates unstable. The suicide literature includes studies that emphasize long-term risk factors after suicide attempts, including a 37-year follow-up period, and studies that note attrition and missing data as problems in long-term follow-up [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In suicide risk research, long-term follow-up is necessary to capture completed suicide, but it is also vulnerable to dropout and missing data, which can distort estimates. The cited evidence on suicide attempters’ long-term survival also notes that only about 10% of suicide attempt survivors die by suicide later, and that follow-up is critical for capturing the true long-term risk [N4-R2]. In UHR cohorts, attrition is especially important because the study population may be followed for many years, and missing data can reduce the effective sample size and introduce bias. The evidence also suggests that longer follow-up can reveal changes in suicide risk over time, but that attrition reduces the reliability of estimates [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

Taken together, the UHR suicide estimation problem is therefore not just a question of whether suicide is rare; it is a question of how rare it is, how well it is captured by the study design, and how much the study must follow participants to observe meaningful events. Because UHR groups are at higher risk than the general population but still have relatively low completed suicide rates, any prevalence estimate is subject to large variance, wide confidence intervals, and instability when the base rate is low. The combination of rare outcomes, ascertainment limitations, and attrition means that observed prevalence may not reflect true prevalence well, especially in long-term follow-up studies [N2-R2][N3-F3][N4-R3][N4-R5].

## Why the low base rate of completed suicide in ultra-high-risk (UHR) groups makes long-term suicide prevalence hard to estimate reliably

The core reason the low base rate of completed suicide in UHR groups makes long-term suicide prevalence hard to estimate reliably is that rare outcomes are inherently difficult to measure accurately when they are rare, and UHR cohorts introduce additional design and measurement challenges. The evidence shows that UHR individuals are at higher risk of suicidality than many clinical groups, including help-seekers who do not meet UHR criteria and first-episode psychosis patients [N3-F3]. At the same time, completed suicide remains rare enough that the absolute number of observed events is small, even in a group that is otherwise at elevated risk [N3-F3][N2-R2]. That combination creates a problem: the outcome is rare, the population is not the same as the general population, and the study must follow participants for a long time to capture meaningful events [N3-F3][N4-R3].

### 1) Low base rate increases variance and reduces statistical power

When the base rate is low, the number of observed events is small, and statistical power decreases. The branch report explains that sample size critically affects study design and that inadequate sample size is one of the main statistical errors in research [N1-F1][N1-R3]. It also states that sample size determination is the act of choosing the number of observations to include in a statistical sample, and that statistically incorrect sample size can result in inadequate results and wasted resources [N1-F1][N1-R5]. This directly supports the idea that low base rate increases variance and reduces power because the precision of the estimate depends on the number of observed events, not just the total sample size [N1-F1][N1-R5].

The rare-event literature reinforces this point. It notes that poor AUC behavior—as measured by empirical bias, variability of cross-validated AUC estimates, and empirical coverage of confidence intervals—is driven by the number of events, not event rate [N5-F2]. In other words, when the base rate is low, the estimate has less certainty, and the confidence interval becomes wider because there is less information [N5-F2]. The same source also states that poor AUC behavior can be driven by the number of events even in large samples, reinforcing that low base rate matters more than sample size alone [N5-F2]. For prevalence estimation, this means that a low base rate makes the estimate unstable and harder to interpret.

### 2) Confidence intervals widen and estimates become unstable

The branch report says that confidence intervals widen and estimates become unstable when the base rate is low [N7]. That is exactly what the rare-event evidence supports: poor AUC behavior is driven by the number of events, and confidence intervals and cross-validated estimates become more variable when the number of events is small [N5-F2]. In practical terms, this means that prevalence estimates from UHR cohorts are less precise and more sensitive to random variation. If only a few suicide events are observed, the confidence interval around the estimate is wide, and the estimate can change substantially with small sample changes or missing data [N5-F2].

This instability matters because prevalence is often used to compare groups or to infer risk. If the confidence interval is wide, the estimate may not be reliable enough to draw conclusions about whether the observed rate is truly different from zero or from a control group [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that researchers can overstate analysis results and that excessive interpretation of limited or insignificant results is a common statistical error [N1-F1]. So even when a study reports a non-zero rate, the estimate may not be reliable if the confidence interval is too wide.

### 3) Rare-event models and prevalence estimation methods behave poorly under low base rates

The branch report explains that rare-event models and prevalence estimation methods behave poorly under low base rates [N7]. The evidence on rare-event prediction shows that estimating and reporting prediction model performance in the rare event setting presents several challenges, and that AUC is often misleading in rare-event settings [N5-R1][N5-R2]. It also states that poor AUC behavior is driven by the number of events, not event rate, and that other measures such as sensitivity and specificity depend on the number of events or non-events, while positive predictive value and accuracy depend on event rate even in large samples [N5-F2]. This matters for prevalence estimation because prevalence is often estimated using similar principles: if the base rate is low, the estimator has less power to distinguish true signals from noise, and its confidence intervals are less reliable.

In UHR cohorts, this means that methods designed for common outcomes may not work well when the outcome is rare. For example, a study may look statistically significant, but the estimate may be driven by a small number of events rather than a strong effect [N5-F2]. This is especially important for long-term prevalence estimates because follow-up is needed to capture completed suicide, and the number of observed events is small even with large sample sizes [N5-F2]. Therefore, prevalence estimation under low base rates is not just a question of statistical significance; it is a question of whether the estimate is precise enough to be useful.

## Why the low base rate of completed suicide in ultra-high-risk (UHR) groups makes long-term suicide prevalence hard to estimate reliably

The core reason the low base rate of completed suicide in UHR groups makes long-term suicide prevalence hard to estimate reliably is that rare outcomes are inherently difficult to measure accurately when they are rare, and UHR cohorts introduce additional design and measurement challenges. The evidence shows that UHR individuals are at higher risk of suicidality than many clinical groups, including help-seekers who do not meet UHR criteria and first-episode psychosis patients [N3-F3]. At the same time, completed suicide remains rare enough that the absolute number of observed events is small, even in a group that is otherwise at elevated risk [N3-F3][N2-R2]. That combination creates a problem: the outcome is rare, the population is not the same as the general population, and the study must follow participants for a long time to capture meaningful events [N3-F3][N4-R3].

### 1) Low base rate increases variance and reduces statistical power

When the base rate is low, the number of observed events is small, and statistical power decreases. The branch report explains that sample size critically affects study design and that inadequate sample size is one of the main statistical errors in research [N1-F1][N1-R3]. It also states that sample size determination is the act of choosing the number of observations to include in a statistical sample, and that statistically incorrect sample size can result in inadequate results and wasted resources [N1-F1][N1-R5]. This directly supports the idea that low base rate increases variance and reduces power because the precision of the estimate depends on the number of observed events, not just the total sample size [N1-F1][N1-R5].

The rare-event literature reinforces this point. It notes that poor AUC behavior—as measured by empirical bias, variability of cross-validated AUC estimates, and empirical coverage of confidence intervals—is driven by the number of events, not event rate [N5-F2]. In other words, when the base rate is low, the estimate has less certainty, and the confidence interval becomes wider because there is less information [N5-F2]. The same source also states that poor AUC behavior can be driven by the number of events even in large samples, reinforcing that low base rate matters more than sample size alone [N5-F2]. For prevalence estimation, this means that a low base rate makes the estimate unstable and harder to interpret.

### 2) Confidence intervals widen and estimates become unstable

The branch report says that confidence intervals widen and estimates become unstable when the base rate is low [N7]. That is exactly what the rare-event evidence supports: poor AUC behavior is driven by the number of events, and confidence intervals and cross-validated estimates become more variable when the number of events is small [N5-F2]. In practical terms, this means that prevalence estimates from UHR cohorts are less precise and more sensitive to random variation. If only a few suicide events are observed, the confidence interval around the estimate is wide, and the estimate can change substantially with small sample changes or missing data [N5-F2].

This instability matters because prevalence is often used to compare groups or to infer risk. If the confidence interval is wide, the estimate may not be reliable enough to draw conclusions about whether the observed rate is truly different from zero or from a control group [N1-F1][N5-F2]. The evidence also emphasizes that researchers can overstate analysis results and that excessive interpretation of limited or insignificant results is a common statistical error [N1-F1]. So even when a study reports a non-zero rate, the estimate may not be reliable if the confidence interval is too wide.

### 3) Rare-event models and prevalence estimation methods behave poorly under low base rates

The branch report explains that rare-event models and prevalence estimation methods behave poorly under low base rates [N7]. The evidence on rare-event prediction shows that estimating and reporting prediction model performance in the rare event setting presents several challenges, and that AUC is often misleading in rare-event settings [N5-R1][N5-R2]. It also states that poor AUC behavior is driven by the number of events, not event rate, and that other measures such as sensitivity and specificity depend on the number of events or non-events, while positive predictive value and accuracy depend on event rate even in large samples [N5-F2]. This matters for prevalence estimation because prevalence is often estimated using similar principles: if the base rate is low, the estimator has less power to distinguish true signals from noise, and its confidence intervals are less reliable.

In UHR cohorts, this means that methods designed for common outcomes may not work well when the outcome is rare. For example, a study may look statistically significant, but the estimate may be driven by a small number of events rather than a strong effect [N5-F2]. This is especially important for long-term prevalence estimates because follow-up is needed to capture completed suicide, and the number of observed events is small even with large sample sizes [N5-F2]. Therefore, prevalence estimation under low base rates is not just a question of statistical significance; it is a question of whether the estimate is precise enough to be useful.

### 4) Suicide is rare in UHR groups despite high risk

The branch report on UHR suicide prevalence says suicide is rare in UHR groups despite high risk [N8]. The evidence on UHR suicide risk literature shows that suicide is a major risk factor in UHR individuals, especially those at risk for psychosis, and that suicidality is typically higher in UHR groups than in other clinical cohorts [N3-F3]. At the same time, the suicide literature shows that suicide is rare enough that studies must rely on careful ascertainment to capture events accurately [N2-R2]. The cited prospective cohort study on UHR individuals also notes that there is limited research on suicidality in this population and that most prior work has been cross-sectional and Western-focused [N3-F3]. This matters because it shows that UHR groups are not representative of the general population and that suicide is rare enough that even a population at elevated risk may not produce many completed suicide events [N3-F3][N2-R2].

### 5) Ascertainment bias and underreporting affect observed prevalence

The branch report on UHR suicide prevalence says that ascertainment bias and underreporting affect observed prevalence [N8]. The suicide measurement evidence shows that suicide is rare and that studies must rely on careful ascertainment to capture events accurately [N2-R2]. In UHR cohorts, weak ascertainment can lead to underascertainment, while strong linkage to death registries or electronic health records can improve detection [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The branch report on prevalence measurement also explains that case ascertainment and linkage determine whether an event is counted, and that prevalence differs from incidence because prevalence measures the total number of cases in a population at a given time, while incidence measures the number of new cases that occur during a defined period [N9].

This distinction is important for interpreting observed prevalence. If a study counts only the cases that are captured through linkage or clinical records, it may miss true events, especially when suicide is rare and the source data are incomplete [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4]. The evidence also notes that suicide-related clinical research expects adverse events such as suicidal ideation and behavior to occur, which suggests that ascertainment is not always perfect in suicide-focused research [N6-R2]. Therefore, observed prevalence can be misleading if case ascertainment is weak or if linkage is incomplete [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### 6) Follow-up duration and attrition affect long-term prevalence estimates

The branch report on UHR suicide prevalence says that follow-up duration and attrition affect long-term prevalence estimates [N8]. The suicide literature includes studies that emphasize long-term risk factors after suicide attempts, including a 37-year follow-up period, and studies that note attrition and missing data as problems in long-term follow-up [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. In suicide risk research, long-term follow-up is necessary to capture completed suicide, but it is also vulnerable to dropout and missing data, which can distort estimates [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5].

The branch report on practical implications further explains that longer follow-up can increase the chance of observing events, but only if the cohort remains intact; shorter follow-up may miss events, while larger sample size may improve precision only if it includes enough events [N10]. The evidence on rare-event prediction also shows that performance metrics such as AUC are driven by the number of events, while sensitivity is driven by the number of events and specificity by the number of non-events [N5-F2]. This means that in UHR cohorts, follow-up length matters because it determines how many events can be observed over time, while sample size matters because it determines the precision of the estimate [N10][N5-F2]. Long follow-up is needed to capture rare events, but attrition reduces the effective sample size and weakens the estimate [N4-R3][N4-R5].

### 7) What determines whether an event is counted

The branch report on prevalence measurement says that prevalence in UHR cohorts is measured by identifying completed suicide events, but the definition of a completed suicide event and the quality of case ascertainment determine whether an event is counted [N9]. The broader suicide literature shows that suicide can be studied through cohort studies and autopsied cohorts, suggesting that suicide events are often identified through systematic ascertainment rather than casual reporting [N2-R2]. In suicide-focused assessment, the goal is to determine the level of suicide risk rather than to predict future suicide, and suicide-related clinical research expects adverse events such as suicidal ideation and behavior to occur [N6-R2].

This matters for prevalence because suicide is not always measured as a simple yes/no event. It depends on how the study defines the outcome and how it captures it. In UHR cohorts, completed suicide is especially sensitive to ascertainment, linkage, and study design [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4]. If the study defines suicide too narrowly or relies on incomplete linkage, it may undercount true events [N2-R2][N6-R3]. If it defines suicide too broadly, it may include events that are not actually completed suicide [N2-R2]. Therefore, observed prevalence is shaped not only by the true risk, but also by how the outcome is defined and captured [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### 8) Prevalence differs from incidence, and that matters

The branch report on prevalence measurement explains that prevalence differs from incidence and why that matters [N9]. Prevalence measures the total number of cases in a population at a given time, while incidence measures the number of new cases that occur during a defined period [N2-R2][N6-R4]. In UHR cohorts, this distinction is important because the question is not just how many people die by suicide, but also how the study defines the time window in which events are counted [N2-R2][N6-R4].

For long-term prevalence estimates, incidence is often more informative than prevalence because it reflects the rate of new suicide events during follow-up, while prevalence reflects the proportion of individuals who have experienced suicide over the study period. The suicide measurement evidence also highlights that suicide can be rare enough that follow-up duration and attrition affect the observed count, which is why incidence is often more informative than prevalence in studies of rare events [N2-R2][N4-R3]. In UHR cohorts, therefore, prevalence is especially sensitive to ascertainment, linkage, and study design, and the definition of a completed suicide event can shape the observed rate more than the true risk [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4].

### 9) Practical implications for study design and interpretation

The branch report on practical implications says that more reliable study designs are those that prioritize sufficient follow-up, robust case ascertainment, and appropriate sample size [N10]. The evidence on sample size and power explains that sample size critically affects study design and that inadequate sample size is a major source of error [N1-F1][N1-R3]. It also stresses that sample size calculation requires many assumptions and should focus on the minimal clinically important difference, which means studies should be powered to detect meaningful effects rather than just any statistically significant result [N1-R2][N1-R3]. For rare outcomes, this is especially important because the number of observed events determines statistical power, not just the total sample size [N5-F2].

In UHR suicide research, a non-significant result may reflect low power, measurement limitations, or true absence of effect, and should not be interpreted as proof of no risk without careful consideration of study design, follow-up, and ascertainment [N1-F1][N5-F2].

Sample size and follow-up length matter differently for rare outcomes. The evidence on rare-event prediction shows that performance metrics such as AUC are driven by the number of events, while sensitivity is driven by the number of events and specificity by the number of non-events [N5-F2]. It also states that positive predictive value and accuracy depend on event rate even in large samples [N5-F2]. In other words, for rare outcomes, longer follow-up can increase the chance of observing events, but only if the cohort remains intact; shorter follow-up may miss events, while larger sample size may improve precision only if it includes enough events [N10][N5-F2].

### Final synthesis

In summary, the low base rate of completed suicide in UHR groups makes long-term suicide prevalence hard to estimate reliably for several reasons. First, a low base rate increases variance and reduces statistical power because the estimate is based on a small number of events [N1-F1][N1-R5]. Second, confidence intervals widen and estimates become unstable because there is less information when the outcome is rare [N5-F2]. Third, rare-event models and prevalence estimation methods behave poorly under low base rates because the usual performance metrics are not designed for such settings [N5-R1][N5-R2]. Fourth, suicide is rare in UHR groups despite high risk, which means that even a population at elevated risk may not produce many completed suicide events [N3-F3][N2-R2]. Fifth, ascertainment bias and underreporting can distort observed prevalence if case ascertainment is weak or linkage is incomplete [N2-R2][N6-R3][N6-R4]. Sixth, follow-up duration and attrition affect long-term prevalence estimates because longer follow-up is needed to capture rare events, but attrition reduces the effective sample size and weakens the estimate [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R5]. Seventh, prevalence differs from incidence, and that distinction matters because prevalence reflects the total number of cases, while incidence reflects the rate of new cases during follow-up [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Eighth, study design matters: reliable designs prioritize sufficient follow-up, robust case ascertainment, and appropriate sample size [N10]. Ninth, non-significant or small effects should be interpreted cautiously because low power or measurement limitations may explain them [N1-F1][N5-F2]. Tenth, sample size and follow-up length matter differently for rare outcomes: follow-up increases the chance of observing events, while sample size improves precision only when it includes enough events [N10][N5-F2].

Taken together, the low base rate in UHR groups creates a triple burden: small observed events, unstable estimates, and design limitations that make it hard to distinguish true risk from measurement error or chance [N1-F1][N5-F2][N2-R2][N4-R3].
